questions.question_text: Write the value of $\pi$ correct to $4$ decimal places.

options.why: Cut the decimal off after four places instead of rounding the fifth digit $9$ up.
Rounded to three decimal places first and then padded the result with a zero.
Transposed the last two digits when recalling $3.1416$ from memory.

questions.question_text: A circle has circumference $C$, diameter $d$ and radius $r$. Which calculation gives $\pi$?

options.why: Inverted the ratio, dividing the diameter by the circumference to get $0.318\ldots$
Used the radius in place of the diameter, which gives $2\pi$ instead of $\pi$.
Multiplied the two measurements instead of dividing one by the other.

questions.solution_text:
$\pi$ is the constant ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter.
$\pi = \frac{C}{d}$

questions.question_text: Circle A has diameter $3$ cm and circle B has diameter $30$ cm. How does $C \div d$ for circle B compare with $C \div d$ for circle A?

options.why: Assumed the ratio grows with the circle, because circle B is $10$ times as wide.
Assumed dividing by a larger diameter must make the ratio smaller.
Scaled the ratio by the square of the factor the diameter was multiplied by.

questions.solution_text:
Circle B has $10$ times the diameter, and also $10$ times the circumference.
The two factors of $10$ cancel in the division, so both circles give $\pi$.
It is the same.

questions.question_text: The distance around a circle is about how many times its diameter?

options.why: Compared the circumference with the radius instead of the diameter, which gives $2\pi$.
Treated $\pi$ as exactly $3$ rather than a little more than $3$.
Divided the diameter by the circumference instead of the circumference by the diameter.

questions.solution_text:
$C \div d = \pi = 3.14159\ldots$ for every circle.
The distance around is just over $3$ times the diameter.

questions.question_text:
Four circular objects were measured.
$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Object} & C\text{ (cm)} & d\text{ (cm)} \\ \hline A & 25.1 & 8.0 \\ B & 47.1 & 15.0 \\ C & 62.8 & 16.0 \\ D & 34.5 & 11.0 \end{array}$
For which object must a measurement be wrong?

options.why: Chose the object with the smallest measurements, assuming small circles give unreliable ratios.
Divided $d$ by $C$ to get $0.32$ and judged that this was too far from $\pi$.
Rounded $34.5 \div 11.0 = 3.136$ down to $3.1$ and judged it too far from $3.14$.

questions.solution_text:
A: $\frac{25.1}{8.0} = 3.1375$
B: $\frac{47.1}{15.0} = 3.14$
C: $\frac{62.8}{16.0} = 3.925$
D: $\frac{34.5}{11.0} = 3.136\ldots$
Every circle should give a ratio close to $3.14$, but object C gives $3.93$.
Object C has a wrong measurement.
